jobs.prompt:
docs(cpp): audit coroutine and callback lifetimes across the application modules (report with proposed fixes)

CONTEXT (you have no other context than this prompt and the repository)
You start from branch `agent-jobs/cppgw-suite-repair-20261118-44210723939-1` of ubiquity/ai.ubq.fi: a known-good state of `cpp/gateway/`, a C++20 port of this repository's TypeScript gateway (`src/`, `serve.ts`), with a JavaScript-style runtime layer (`include/uos/rt`, `src/rt`, `src/runtime`), vendored simdjson and simdutf (`cpp/gateway/third_party/`), ICU for Unicode, and about 442 standalone test binaries (`cpp/gateway/tests/**/*_test.cpp`). On this state the release build passes its whole suite on Linux ARM64. The native gateway is already 1.2-1.9x faster than the TypeScript gateway on Bun end to end and uses about a third of the memory (`cpp/gateway/docs/findings/cppgw-perf-request-path-20261117.md`). Every deployment target is 64-bit ARM: an Arch Linux ARM VPS, an Apple Silicon Mac and a Raspberry Pi.

OWNER POLICY (binding): generic functionality comes from mature open-source or standard libraries; exact parity with Bun's quirks and error wording is NOT required; less first-party code is preferred. What must hold: the gateway's functional behaviour (wire formats, status codes, stored data, authentication and validation decisions, accounting) and security never getting weaker.

READ FIRST: `cpp/gateway/docs/CI.md` (portable build-and-test driver; invoke it as `bash cpp/gateway/tools/ci-build.sh ...`, the file lacks its executable bit), `cpp/gateway/docs/BUILD.md`, `cpp/gateway/docs/RUNTIME.md`, `cpp/gateway/docs/OSS-REPLACEMENT-PLAN.md`, `cpp/gateway/PORTING.md` (its coroutine rules are mandatory; its "Host safety" and "compile only through tools/unit.sh" rules apply to the authors' server, not to your disposable runner; where it demands exact Bun parity, the owner policy above wins). `python3 cpp/gateway/tools/links.py <test>` prints a test's application sources; every `src/rt/*.cpp` and the vendored libraries link into every test.

About ten other agents are changing other parts of `cpp/gateway` on their own branches at the same time (URL, HTTP parsing, regex, WebSocket, passkey CBOR and ASN.1, BigInt, date/console/filesystem/env/headers helpers, the stored-value reader, a test-suite repair). Your branch will be merged with theirs: stay strictly inside your OWNED PATHS and keep everything else byte-identical.

GENERAL RULES
- The runner holds a model gateway token: never print it or write any credential to a file. Run tests with an empty `HOME`, a fresh `TMPDIR` and no provider variables. No real provider traffic: use local mocks only.
- Do not edit `.github/` (unless your task says so), the TypeScript, or `cpp/` outside `cpp/gateway/`. Do not delete or weaken tests.
- Model connections can drop: create your report file in the first minutes and commit small steps often (the tree must build at each commit). Leave no build output, binaries or downloads in the checkout.
- Report file: `cpp/gateway/docs/findings/<job id>.md`: what you did, exact commands, real counts and measurements, what is unfinished, defects found outside your paths (report, do not fix). End your final message with the same summary.

YOUR MACHINE: GitHub-hosted Linux x64 runner (Ubuntu 26.04, 4 CPUs, 16 GB, sudo, network), borrowed compute: the product is ARM64, so write nothing x64-specific. `sudo apt-get install -y clang ninja-build pkg-config libboost-json-dev libboost-container-dev libssl-dev libsqlite3-dev zlib1g-dev libicu-dev libbrotli-dev libzstd-dev` gives Clang 21 and Boost 1.90, enough to build this tree. Two fixtures assert ARM64-only platform support and fail on x64 by design (`permissions_linux_test`, `runtime_native_startup_test`).

OWNED PATHS (you may create or edit only these, plus your report)
- `cpp/gateway/docs/findings/cppgw-coroutine-lifetime-audit-20261118.md`, `cpp/gateway/analysis/lifetime/` (new: scripts and the machine-readable site list)

TASK
This code base is a mechanical port of asynchronous TypeScript onto C++20 coroutines (Boost.Asio awaitables behind JavaScript-style `Promise`/`Task` wrappers in `include/uos/rt/async.hpp`). In JavaScript closures keep their captured state alive; in C++ they do not, and one confirmed memory-safety defect of this class was already found and fixed (`src/admin/kernel.cpp`: coroutine lambdas capturing handler locals, awaited through a fail-fast `rt::all` that does not cancel siblings, so a still-pending sibling resumed into a destroyed frame; see `cpp/gateway/docs/findings/cppgw-clang-tidy-audit-20261117.md` and the rule added to `PORTING.md`). An earlier audit judged 25 further sites safe, but it was done quickly and before large refactors. Do a systematic, tool-assisted audit of ALL first-party code under `cpp/gateway/src` and `cpp/gateway/include` for lifetime hazards across suspension points: (a) coroutine lambdas with captures (by reference or by value: the closure object itself must outlive the coroutine) whose returned task can outlive the enclosing scope (passed to `rt::all`/`allSettled`/`race`, stored, detached with `spawn`, returned); (b) coroutine functions taking reference or `string_view`/`span` parameters that are used after the first `co_await` while the caller may not keep the referent alive; (c) `this` captured in callbacks registered on longer-lived objects (sockets, timers, abort signals, streams) without ownership, and the reverse (ownership cycles that leak: several were found by sanitizers in `runtime/http*.cpp`, `codex/supervisor_transport.cpp`, `provider/stream_relay.cpp`); (d) iterators or references into containers held across `co_await` while another coroutine can mutate the container; (e) structured bindings or temporaries bound directly to a `co_await` expression (a known GCC 12 miscompile pattern the port forbids). Use clang-tidy with `cppcoreguidelines-avoid-capturing-lambda-coroutines`, `cppcoreguidelines-avoid-reference-coroutine-parameters`, `misc-coroutine-hostile-raii`, `bugprone-dangling-handle`, `bugprone-use-after-move` and the clang static analyzer over every translation unit (the tree has `cpp/gateway/.clang-tidy` and `tools/tidy.sh`), plus your own AST or grep-based finders for the patterns the checks miss; then READ every reported site and classify it: DEFECT (give the failing interleaving in two lines and a minimal diff), SAFE (one line why: who owns what), or UNCLEAR. Where you can, confirm a DEFECT by building a focused test under AddressSanitizer that drives the interleaving through the real code (keep such tests out of the checkout; put a description and the command in the report). Do not change production code or tests: other agents own those files; the maintainer will dispatch fixes from your list. Rank defects: memory safety on a request path first.

DONE WHEN
The report contains the tool versions and exact commands, the full site list with a verdict for every site (also as `analysis/lifetime/sites.json`), a ranked DEFECT list with proposed diffs, and counts per class.
